newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky welcomes metalworkers deal on pay.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky welcomes metalworkers deal on pay.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky on Sunday welcomed a weekend deal between the country's metalworkers' union and employers, ending a dispute over pay and conditions threatening to disrupt the industry.
"With this agreement, the social partners have demonstrated that they are fully able to carry out their responsibilities," Vranitzky told Austrian television.
Austrian governments since 1945 have laid heavy emphasis on a system of industrial relations based on a so-called "social partnership" between government, unions and employers.
The country has experienced few strikes since World War Two, despite recent austerity measures introduced by the government to cut a yawning budget deficit.
Thousands of workers belonging to the metal and engineering trade union took to the streets of Vienna on Wednesday in a rare demonstration to back calls for a pay rise.
Union and employers' leaders thrashed out a deal late on Saturday evening giving workers who come under the umbrella of the industry's collective agreement a rise of 2.8 percent from January 1, 1997.
Metal workers outside the collective agreement, usually those on higher pay, would receive a 1.8 percent increase.
Inflation in Austria in October was at 2.1 percent.

Negotiations also focused on working out a framework for more flexible working hours for the industry's 100,000 workers, with a final settlement pinning the working-hours ceiling at nine hours a day, 45 hours a week.
Rudolf Nuernberger, leader of the Metall-Bergbau-Energie union, described the deal as "a comprise in the interests of social peace".
The main employers' negotiator Eduard Leischko said the two sides had agreed on the package after hours of sometimes difficult talks but added that the result was "an acceptable solution".

Austria's metal industry has averted the increasingly difficult relations seen in neighbouring Germany between employers and unions. IG Metall, Germany's huge metal and engineering trade union, on Thursday attacked as unreasonable an employer call for a five-year wage freeze in the sector just before the two sides enter key negotiations.

IG Metall has indicated it would accept a wage increase in line with inflation next year, but only if accompanied by expenditure to protect employment levels in the sector, where thousands of workers are laid off each month.

Regional negotiations aimed at finding a deal on wages and labour costs are due to start in the steel-making region of North-Rhine Westphalia on Monday, after attempts to secure a nationwide deal failed last month.
